newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Rival marches planned in Kinshasa despite ban.
newsitem.headline: Rival marches planned in Kinshasa despite ban.

text.p: Opponents and supporters of newly installed President Laurent Kabila plan rival marches in the Democratic Republic of Congo's capital on Friday in defiance of a government ban.

Kabila took office in Kinshasa on Thursday, promising to hold elections in April 1999 and eradicate the legacy of ousted president Mobutu Sese Seko, who was driven out by a seven-month military campaign.

But among the tens of thousands of people who heard Kabila pledge democratic intentions were students who chanted slogans accusing him of trying to squash democracy and rule with the help of troops from tiny neighbour Rwanda.
The United States welcomed Kabila's pledge on elections, saying a two-year transition period seemed reasonable.

Troops firing bursts of automatic gunfire over the heads of student supporters of veteran opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi on Wednesday broke up a demonstration against his exclusion from government and the presence of Rwandans who helped secure Kabila's swift victory.
"It's up to the people to make Kabila go," Tshisekedi told about 2,000 militants outside his house on Thursday. "If the people want to end dictatorship it is up to them and not me."
His supporters plan to start their protest march at 8 a.m. (0700 GMT) outside the railway station in the city centre.
State-run radio and circulated leaflets gave news of a rival march to support Kabila, which is scheduled to start at 10 a.m. (0900 GMT).
Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo has banned political activity and public demonstrations, citing the need to preserve public order.

On Wednesday, Kabila decreed himself sweeping powers to run the country until the adoption of a new transitional constitution by a promised constituent council as part of the plan to hold elections by April 1999.

He assured the crowd in the stadium where he was sworn in that the two-year timetable would be respected and said it would be unaffected by foreign pressure. He made no mention of the elections being multi-party.
"We believe this is a positive step (by Kabila)", U.S. State Department spokesman John Dinger told reporters in Washington.

"We have said that we hope that elections are held sooner rather than later. We have to understand that Congo confronts real and severe problems... a two-year period in that context does not seem unreasonable to us," Dinger added.
Kabila also got expressions of confidence for his plans for democracy from heads of five neighbouring countries -- Angola, Rwanda, Burundi, Uganda and Zambia -- who attended the swearing-in.

After more than three decades of misrule by Mobutu and a corrupt elite, the former Zaire, with vast reserves of copper, cobalt, zinc, gold, diamonds and other minerals, has been left as one of the poorest countries in the world.
Under pressure from the West to introduce democracy in 1990, Mobutu gave up absolute power and pursued a programme aimed at holding multi-party elections.
But they were repeatedly stalled and Zaire sank further into political chaos and economic mess.

Kabila on Thursday pledged to rebuild the state by abolishing dual currency zones, aiming to eradicate unemployment and improving dilapidated transport networks across the vast nation. The one-time Maoist made no mention of free-market reform.
The U.N. Security Council, alarmed by reports of massacres of Rwandan refugees, called on Thursday for an immediate end to violence against the exiles in Kabila's Congo.

The U.S.-initiated statement, read at a formal meeting, also called for the "withdrawal of all external forces" and asked for peaceful transitional arrangements leading to the holding of "democratic and free elections with the participation of all parties".
Diplomats said the statement was meant to give backing to U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan at the Organisation of African Unity summit next week and send a warning to Kabila.

The main U.N. thrust was human rights for the refugees, remnants of more than one million Hutus who fled Rwanda in 1994 to escape possible reprisals for the genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
"It (the council) is particularly concerned by reports that refugees in the east of the country are being systematically killed," the statement said.
"It calls for an immediate end to the violence against refugees in the country," it added.

The 15-member council called "in the strongest terms for complete cooperation with the U.N. mission investigating reports of massacres, other atrocities and violations of international law in the country".
Investigators have been refused access so far to suspected mass graves.
